newsitem.title: JORDAN: Uday's attacker could be one of many enemies.
newsitem.headline: Uday's attacker could be one of many enemies.

text.p: Whoever shot Saddam Hussein's eldest son Uday in a posh Baghdad suburb on Thursday could have been one of the many enemies he had made -- both within Iraq's inner circle of power and in the exiled opposition.

The attacker failed to kill the man widely believed to be the president's heir apparent but the shooting exposed a hole in Baghdad's usually watertight security and highlighted the threats that exist to Saddam's rule.
"Whatever the motives, personal or political, it's a warning to the regime," one Iraqi opposition figure in Jordan said.
Details of the shooting, in Baghdad's smart Mansour district on Thursday evening, were scarce.
Iraqi television said Uday, 32, was wounded while driving his car but his health was "not a matter of concern" after the "cowardly attack". It said he was taken to hospital.

"The fact that they announced it on television suggests everything's under control," said one diplomat who follows Iraqi affairs. "If he were in danger or there were other incidents, we wouldn't see this openness."
"But it's a rare piece of encouragement for (Saddam's) opponents," he added.
None of the disparate Iraqi opposition groups in exile has claimed responsibility for the attack.

Iraqi media said Uday was taken to Baghdad's Ibn Sina hospital after the attack but have not shown any pictures of him there, raising some speculation that his wounds were more serious than reported or even that he died in the attack.
Diplomats said the shooting may have been a personal attack on the president's high-profile son, who runs his own newspaper and television channel.
Uday's influence goes far beyond his modest official title -- chairman of the Iraqi Olympic Committee.

Diplomats say Uday, pictured in newspapers sporting designer stubble, snappy suits and sunglasses, is conspicuously fond of high living in a country where most people have been reduced to hand-to-mouth poverty by six years of stringent U.N. sanctions, imposed for Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
Although his younger brother Qusay heads Iraq's special security forces, Uday has also muscled his way into power, upsetting people within and outside the ruling circle.

Diplomats say his rivalry with Saddam's son-in-law Lieutenant-General Hussein Hassan Kamel, mastermind of Iraq's secret weapons procurement programmes, led to Kamel's defection to Jordan in August last year.
They say Kamel took fright when Uday shot and wounded Saddam's half-brother Watban Ibrahim al-Hassan.
Uday met the penitent Kamel on the Iraqi border seven months later when he returned from exile. Within three days Kamel was shot dead.
Since the defection opposition groups say Uday emerged as the informal crown prince of Iraq, though diplomats in Baghdad say Saddam used the turmoil around him to reassert his own absolute authority.
A wave of arrests in Baghdad over the summer led to reports of a coup attempt, but there are few signs that Saddam's 25-year grip on power has waned.

Diplomats say Uday, often seen about town on Thursday nights at the start of the Moslem weekend, was a far easier target than his father, who has made only a handful of public appearances in the last year.
Uday, a loose cannon in Saddam's inner clique of close relatives, was briefly out of favour after he beat to death one of his father's favourite servants in November 1988.
He later married the teenage daughter of Barzan Ibrahim al-Tikriti, another of Saddam's half-brothers, only to reject her and send her back to her father.
His former father-in-law compared Uday last year to the two Iraqi defectors as "greedy and unfit for power."
